newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asian architects warn of heartless mega-cities.
newsitem.headline: Asian architects warn of heartless mega-cities.

text.p: Asia's booming growth is leaving an unpleasant stamp on its cities as unchecked construction leads to urban sprawls blind to the character of their pasts, major architects in the region say.
Architects from 15 countries across Asia meeting in Jakarta this week warned that rapid growth in the region's urban centres threatened to make them unliveable.

"City with a soul", the name chosen by the Asian Congress of Architects for its seventh biannual meeting, is a warning to governments and developers to think of more than just profit margins, said congress chairman Michael Sumarijanto.
"Developers are thinking piecemeal," Sumarijanto told Reuters. "First the new development is built, and the infrastructure comes later."

Sumarijanto said the problem faced by Indonesia was similar to those in many fast-growing Asian economies. With average economic growth of eight percent a year, developers put a premium on size and speed of construction, disregarding any overall cohesive plan.

"The regulations which govern development cannot keep pace with development itself," Sumarijanto said. "Unless the super (apartment) blocks are controlled by very clear urban guidelines, then each will become enclosed on its own."
Tay Kheng Soon, a Singaporean architect, said Asian cities were in danger of losing their cultural heritage because of the burgeoning trend toward mass construction.

"Calls for respect for tradition lack any compelling force," he told the congress. "Asian cities and architecture are increasingly characterised by dramatic imported architectural statements, mainly from the United States."
Asian architects are, however, beginning to promote their own cultural values in urban development.
Malaysian architect Ken Yeang was awarded the Architects Regional Council Asia Award (ARCASIA) on Tuesday for combining a Kuala Lumpur office block with elements of a tropical landscape.
"The question is now whether developers are able to understand this," Sumarijanto said.
Developers led by market forces were often unwilling to incur extra costs because of experimentation by the architect, he said.
Those developers invited to join in the debate were adamant that the population pressure on Asian cities meant society had to be pragmatic.

"In Indonesia, more than one million units of houses are needed every year. As for now, the supply is only around 100,000 to 150,000 units a year," Ciputra (Eds: one name), founder of Indonesian property giant PT Ciputra, said.
Ciputra said that because of overpopulation in Asian cities, constructors were now being forced to build self-contained satellite developments on the city boundaries.
Whilst realising that new development was crucial, Sumarijanto said this kind of development could lead to a city losing its character.
"If you lose the soul of a city, you lose the city itself," he said.
